prize_parts.citation: For the development of general palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling, in which ligand design makes amines and aryl halides combine catalytically with free amines and a base

statement.case_for: I keep palladium-catalysed C-N coupling as a single-part prize and my position has not changed since round 1. The chair asks what the Migita/Kosugi work could not do. As I recall the record, the 1983 reaction coupled aryl bromides with aminostannanes: it needed a pre-formed, stoichiometric and toxic tin amide, it was limited to dialkylamines and a narrow set of aryl partners, and it was not a general method that a chemist could pick up. Buchwald first generated the tin amide in situ, and then in 1995 he and Hartwig each removed the tin and used free amines with a base. Subsequent ligand generations (chelating bisphosphines, then bulky biaryl and hindered alkyl phosphines) extended the reaction to primary amines, anilines, aryl chlorides, amides and heterocycles at low loadings. Hartwig's isolation of amido complexes and study of C-N reductive elimination supplied the mechanistic understanding that made ligand design rational. That sequence, from a curiosity to a general catalytic method, is the achievement I would cite, and the wording 'general ... catalysed' places Kosugi and Migita correctly as precursors without adding a third name. The consequence is visible in practice, since the reaction is a standard step in medicinal and process chemistry and in materials such as OLED hole-transport layers. Maturity is not in question after three decades of independent use.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains overlap with the 2010 cross-coupling prize, and I accept that a member who reads it as the same palladium theme will not be moved by my argument alone. The distinction I rely on is chemical: C-C coupling with organometallic partners and C-N coupling with free amines have different elementary-step bottlenecks (transmetalation versus amine binding, deprotonation and C-N reductive elimination), and the ligand problem was different. Whether that is enough is a judgment, not a fact. A second objection, which Aqvist raises, is that it is one bond type and less conceptually broad than degraders or sequencing. I regard breadth of consequence as the better test than breadth of concept, but I recognise it is a values choice. Finally, the Kosugi priority question is a real attribution risk that a two-name prize handles by citation wording and not by resolving it.

responses.point: Linke proposes a two-part prize pairing B057 (Buchwald, Hartwig) with base editing credited to Liu alone, as a fair reflection of the breadth of chemistry.
responses.response: I understand the appeal of showing breadth, but I do not support adding B058 this year. The chair's own case against already names the problems: a decade of history, safety data still accruing, the 2020 CRISPR prize as a close predecessor, and a Liu-only credit that omits Komor and Gaudelli, who did the decisive experiments, and Nishida and Kondo, who worked independently. My round-1 question, what was new chemically beyond fusing known deaminases to Cas proteins, has not been answered in the round-1 exchange, and the answer I expect is protein engineering and directed evolution. A two-part prize should be chosen because each part is strong enough alone, not to balance the field. I would keep B057 alone, and if the committee wants a second part I would prefer to discuss B004 first once its credit is settled.

responses.point: Brzezinski, who lists B057 as an alternative, flags the Kosugi and Migita priority question and asks whether the expert report resolves it; the chair's summary notes that some members see it as a possible priority claim.
responses.response: I think the distinction is technical and concrete, not a matter of taste. The tin-amide chemistry was catalytic in palladium but stoichiometric in a toxic tin reagent, which had to be prepared separately, and its scope was narrow. The advance that made the reaction a general method was the tin-free coupling with free amines and a base and the ligand development that followed, together with the mechanistic work on amido complexes. That is where Buchwald and Hartwig converge, and it is also what the later industrial uptake rests on. I would therefore not add Kosugi: a third name would suggest co-discovery of the general method, which the record does not support. I do agree with you that the citation must say 'general', and that this is the place where the precursor is acknowledged. I would be glad to be corrected by the expert report if it shows that Kosugi's group made the reaction broader than I recall.

responses.point: Aili prefers B004 because degraders embody a new design principle, induced proximity, and she argues that the maturity of B057 does not by itself outweigh a new design principle.
responses.response: I find the induced-proximity principle persuasive, and B004 is my first alternative. I weigh the two cases differently on credit and timing. Aili's own round-1 text concedes that the PROTAC and cereblon glue strands are close to two discoveries, that Handa, Ito, Sakamoto, Kim and Gray all have real claims, and that no degrader is approved. For B057 the claim, the names and the evidence are settled now. I would not call C-N coupling less novel because it is mature. A prize for a method whose effect on how molecules are made is already documented is, to me, more secure than one whose clinical outcome is still open. If the committee agrees on one citation covering PROTACs and glues as a single induced-proximity principle, and on the third name, I would reconsider.

responses.point: Sparr ranks B057 fourth and is unsure whether it is distinct enough from the 2010 cross-coupling prize, but also describes it as mature and mechanistically understood; she prefers condensates (B051).
responses.response: My answer to the chair's question about 2010 is the elementary-step argument given above: different bond, different organometallic intermediates, different ligand requirements. I recognise that you described B057 as mature and mechanistically understood, and I would ask whether, with the cap of three names and the open in vivo questions you identified for condensates, B057 is the configuration you could accept as a clean, defensible outcome even if it is not your first choice. I did not hear a chemical reason in round 1 why the 2010 prize should close the door on a different bond-forming problem, while we have not treated earlier prizes in other areas as closing neighbouring fields.

uncertainties: Whether a majority regards C-N coupling as sufficiently distinct from the 2010 cross-coupling prize.

The detailed priority record, in particular the exact scope of the Kosugi and Migita reaction and who first reported the tin-free coupling, is recalled from memory and not verified; the expert report should confirm it before the citation is fixed.
Current usage figures and the claim of routine use in process chemistry are from memory and unverified.
Whether members who prefer a two-part prize will move to B057 alone, and whether B004 could reach a majority if the credit boundary is settled.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate. I work in synthetic methodology at Lund and none of the candidates is a collaborator, mentor, student or institutional colleague. I disclose field adjacency to Buchwald and Hartwig, whose methods I use and cite, and the shared Lund affiliation with Linke and Sparr, whose preferred candidates do not involve Lund. This is unchanged from round 1.
